title: Sama's kindness
hook: the devoted son's kindness even to the king who shot him (Jataka 540)
tomorrow: a kind act every hour? at work, what even counts?

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta, goodwill to all, a mother's strength with the border taken off. Today that goodwill gets tested by an arrow.

When someone hurts you, the first sentence out of your mouth sets the whole next hour. Here's a first sentence from an old story, one that ends well. A young man named Sama walks down to the river for water, and the deer walk with him, because they aren't afraid of him. His parents are blind, and he's the one who cares for them. A king out hunting sees him and shoots before asking a single thing. The arrow lands. Sama sets down his water jar. And the first thing he says isn't a curse. He asks who shot him, and why. No hate in it.
screen: `THE FIRST SENTENCE.` → `SAMA AT THE RIVER.` → `A KING SHOOTS FIRST.` → `NO CURSE. A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The king steps out, and Sama speaks to him gently. What worries him is his parents: they can't see, and they have no one else. The king is undone, and promises to care for them himself. In the story, Sama falls still, and his parents and a goddess make solemn acts of truth over him, and he wakes. Tradition tells this as the life in which the Bodhisatta perfected loving-kindness. Kind even then. But what does that ask of a person? Two answers live inside the tradition, and both are serious. The first comes from the Simile of the Saw. The Buddha tells his monks that even if bandits were cutting them apart with a two-handled saw, anyone whose mind turned to hate would not be carrying out his teaching. On this view, kindness is an inside job: no ill will, whatever happens. The second view points at Sama himself. He doesn't pretend nothing happened. He tells the king plainly what he has done, and he asks for something: take care of my parents. Elsewhere the Buddha says he speaks what is true and helpful, even when it's unwelcome, if the time is right. On this view, kindness can name the harm. One stresses the heart that won't turn. The other, the voice that still tells the truth.
screen: `THE KING PROMISES TO CARE FOR THEM.` · `VIEW ONE: THE SIMILE OF THE SAW.` · `VIEW TWO: SAMA'S PLAIN WORD.` · `A HEART THAT WON'T TURN; A TRUE VOICE.` · then, large: `KIND EVEN THEN.`

segments.voice: Sit upright with one hand resting over your heart. Bring to mind someone who hurt you, a small hurt, not the biggest, and wish them one plain thing: may you be well. If it sticks, wish yourself well for a while, then try them again.
Sama's kindness: goodwill that didn't turn, even toward the king who had just shot him, and still spoke the truth.
Here's the line: kind even then, with no hate in it and a plain word ready. That's twenty-six.

howItsDone: The Sama Jataka is retold in Theravada Buddhist settings, in sermons, plays and temple paintings, as a story of loving-kindness and of caring for one's parents.

chat.says: trial shift: a lady yelled at me over a mat SHE picked. is kind even then just smiling through it?
options: Not just smiling. No ill will inside, and you can still say what happened.
Yes. Being kind means swallowing it and never saying a word about it.
No. Kindness is for kind people. She yelled, so you're off the hook.
chat.meaning: Sama held no hate toward the king, and still told him plainly what he'd done. Kind even then can be a calm heart and a true word.

notes: For parents: the story has a young man shot by an arrow; it is told gently and ends with him waking and his parents cared for.

Sama Jataka (Jataka 540) paraphrased: Sama cares for his blind parents; deer go with him to the river; King Piliyakkha shoots him while hunting; Sama speaks without anger, asks who shot him and why, and worries for his parents; the king promises to care for them; his parents and the goddess (Bahusodari) make acts of truth and he revives. Confirm the details, especially Sama's first words, and that the acts of truth include both parents and the goddess.
'Tradition tells this as the life in which the Bodhisatta perfected loving-kindness' follows the outline's mapping of the last ten Jatakas to the ten perfections; confirm.
Debate shape: view one (MN 21, the saw simile: no hate even under torture) and view two (Sama's plain word, MN 58's true and timely speech) are both the tradition's own; the lesson ranks neither.
